title: Location unknown for high number of registered sex offenders in Utah
text:
The number of sex offenders listed as non-compliant on Utah’s Sex, Kidnap and Child Abuse registry has climbed again, raising concerns about who is responsible
Salt Lake City Police officers conduct traffic stop on July 24, 2025, and discover non-compliant sex offenders in car. The number of sex offenders listed as non-compliant on Utah’s Sex, Kidnap and Child Abuse registry has climbed again, raising concerns about who is responsible for tracking down those who are not following the rules of the registry regarding where they're living — and whether the state needs a standard enforcement compliance policy, a 2News Investigation found.
The state legislature transferred management of the registry from the Utah Department of Corrections to Utah’s Bureau of Criminal Identification, a division within the Department of Public Safety. It was effective on July 1, 2024. BCI manages the data for the public registry, and it is updated in real time. But BCI does not oversee the enforcement aspects of the registry.
Stephanie Dinsmore, Public Affairs Director for DPS, says, "Consequently, we cannot comment on law enforcement activities or investigations regarding registry non-compliance.
" Enforcement is handled by individual police jurisdictions. Federal authorities monitor those convicted of federal sex crimes, and Adult Probation and Parole is responsible for ensuring probationers and parolees follow registry requirements. A 2News Investigation revealed it's difficult to determine just how targeted each police agency's efforts are at finding non-compliant sex offenders since each agency operates independently. Which begs the question: Should there be a standard policy statewide?
We spoke to a few lawmakers who agreed to look into this. The investigation also found that many jurisdictions come into contact with non-compliant sex offenders when they're homeless or when they're picked up during a traffic stop. For this report, we obtained body camera footage from Salt Lake City Police in two cases from 2025 that illustrate both scenarios. In July 2025, Salt Lake City police pulled over a car with no registration.
In the footage, an officer says, “There’s a sex offender in there too that’s not compliant. ” Officers then focus on a passenger, and one of the officers says, "Front passenger is pretty shady, he gave a fake name. What the hell?
" Another officer says, “That’s a non-compliant sex offender. ” As officers continue checking, one says, “Holy cow, he’s got a lot of warrants — $25,000 for like five counts of providing false info. ” Salt Lake City Police officers conduct traffic stop on July 24, 2025, and discover non-compliant sex offenders in car. Additionally, the footage reveals that the man who sold them the car was also a non-compliant sex offender from another state.
One of the officers running the information from the patrol car says, “Buck out of Wyoming,” with another officer saying, “Who is also a sex offender. ” The man in the back of the car had a knife and was hanging out with non-compliant sex offenders. In another case on Dec. 3, registered sex offender Lee Oliver Larsen was pulled over for an equipment violation at 1100 South 900 West.
Court documents show that while speaking to Larsen, he told Officer Aoki that he had a pipe and a large knife next to the driver's seat. He told Officer Aoki he keeps the knife nearby because he has a lot of "haters," and "wanted people to see it.
" An officer asks, “So where are you living at? ” Larsen responds, “I’m at. ” The officer presses him about an address, asking, “So when I have a sergeant go out to that address where they’re going out right now, they’re gonna say you live there? ” Larsen answers, “Yes.
” The officer asks, “Positive. ” Larsen replies, “Yes. ” Registered Sex Offender Lee Oliver Larsen was pulled over by Salt Lake City Police officers on December 3, 2025. The video shows Larsen, 31, claiming he was living at an uncle’s house, but an officer checks and later says, “He doesn’t live there.
” The officer says, “He lives out of his car,” according to information from Larsen’s brother. The officer tells Larsen, “I’m the state expert when it comes to the sex offender registry and what you are doing ok, is you’re trying to play it. ” Larsen repeatedly insists, “I’m not. ” The officer then says, “You are currently being arrested, ok?
” Registered Sex Offender Lee Oliver Larsen arrested by Salt Lake City Police on December 3, 2025. Larsen is currently incarcerated in the Salt Lake County Metro Jail on possession of a dangerous weapon by a prohibited person, a Third-Degree felony, use or possession of drug paraphernalia, and for not having vehicle insurance stemming from his Dec. 3 arrest.
Larsen was convicted of a violent felony in 2015, that of Forcible Sexual Abuse, listed as attempted, a Third-Degree felony in Eighth Judicial District Court. Data obtained from DPS/BCI shows the number of sex offenders, kidnappers, and child abusers listed as non-compliant has fluctuated but recently increased. On Oct. 1, 2024, 609 were listed as non-compliant. On July 1, 2025, 559 were listed as non-compliant.
As of April 24, 2026, the number was 622. It's important to note that the registry includes sex offenders, kidnappers, and child abusers, and there is no way to isolate sex offenders in the data, though 2News Investigates found the majority are sex offenders. Some of those listed as non-compliant are in ICE custody, and others have been deported, but most were listed as “location unknown. ” For Erin Gehring, a mother of four and a victim, this is concerning.
Gehring told 2News Investigates what happened to both her and her daughter.
“The man just exposed himself to myself and at the time, my baby was 2, so she didn’t know. She still doesn’t know till this day, but come to find out, he’d done it previously, and he lives in a neighborhood with children. ” A review of the 622 listed as non-compliant found that most had no address on file. But 153 did have addresses listed.
After checking those 153 names, we found no identifiable trend with regard to specific cities for those addresses, with addresses spread across Utah. Gehring said, “I think it’s concerning that there’s not a specific jurisdiction assigned to this — that it is easy for them to fall through the cracks. Ultimately, who is responsible for them at the end of the day?
” 2News Investigates contacted numerous law enforcement agencies along the Wasatch Front asking them to provide details about their practices for verifying compliance. Unified Police Sgt. Aymee Race said, “They go once a month with the Special Victims Unit to do sex offender compliance checks for compliant and non-compliant sex offenders. ” Glen Mills, Chief of Staff for the Salt Lake City Police Department, said, “We do compliance checks for those who live within our jurisdiction.
It’s routine. ” Roxeanne Vainuku, Public Information Officer for the West Valley City Police Department, said, “While we previously had funding from the State for proactive compliance checks, that funding is no longer available. ” She added, "Right now, our priority is focusing investigative resources on active cases and supporting victims. We still address violations when they’re identified, but we have to focus where we can have the greatest impact on public safety.
” She also said, “Sex offenders are required to come to our department and check in. We have a detective assigned to manage that process. ” Ogden Police Lt. Shane Keyes said, “We have a dedicated unit that falls within our community policing unit.
We have three or four guys, and that is their main job. ” Utah County Sheriff’s Office Sgt. Ray Ormand said, “Detectives from the Special Victims Unit do compliance checks for sex offenders. ” Weber County Sheriff’s Office Lt.
Charles Creager said, “We have civilian staff who manage our registry. When they get a tip, they then assign it to a detective. We’re forming a proactive unit this summer to do home compliance checks. ”Davis County Sheriff’s Office spokesperson Megan Maybee said, “We actively check registered sex offenders every six months.
” Sgt. Race noted the staffing challenges agencies face.
“It is a big number for a, you know, a small amount of officers in some of these areas — and unfortunately, if they move out of state, that limits it even more. ” Callie Bowen, a mother of three, said, "Something needs to be done, something needs to change because this is not ok,” she said. She added, "There’s only so much you can do as a mom. You want everyone else to kind of have your back.
You want the state to have your back. It sounds like some balls have been dropped somewhere.
" Sgt. Race said parents need to talk with their children.
“Having those conversations with our kids, you know, 'Is anyone doing anything inappropriate? Have you seen anyone acting abnormally or doing things that, you know, mom and dad or mom or just dad have talked to you about? ”Videos and photos show a mountain lion outside a home along the east bench of Salt Lake County, coming close as if to tap on a window.
